idiom_name: hand-written accumulator loop over System.nanoTime() with Thread.sleep pacing
implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM's timing primitives and adds no loop abstraction of its own: java.lang.System.nanoTime() 'returns the current value of the running Java Virtual Machine's high-resolution time source, in nanoseconds', 'can only be used to measure elapsed time and is not related to any other notion of system or wall-clock time', and only differences between two readings are meaningful. Thread.sleep(millis) 'causes the currently executing thread to sleep ... subject to the precision and accuracy of system timers and schedulers'. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - write the driver as a while loop (or a @tailrec method threading the accumulator) over those two calls, and keep the per-step function pure in dt so the simulation itself stays deterministic and testable. When a JVM game framework or UI toolkit is present (libGDX, ScalaFX), let its loop own the cadence and implement only the update callback; cats-effect or fs2 style stacks can express the loop as a temporal stream, but the physics step is still fixed-dt.
pitfalls: System.currentTimeMillis is wall-clock time and jumps when the clock is corrected; nanoTime differences are the interval-safe readings.
Thread.sleep can oversleep and throws InterruptedException; treat it as a hint and keep the loop's timing state authoritative.
JVM GC pauses produce frame spikes out of proportion to allocation size; keep boxing and per-step allocations out of the hot loop.
Scala's @tailrec only applies to the tail-recursive shape; when the accumulator must mutate, a plain while loop is the honest, allocation-free form.
